weeks.objective: Count collections to 100 by making tens and recording leftover ones.

connection.before: Count small collections, with adult support if needed.
connection.after: Compare numbers by their tens and then ones.

explanation: A count tells how many objects are in a collection. Touch or mark each object once and say one number for each. Moving the objects farther apart does not change the total. An empty collection has zero objects.

Ten single counters can be exchanged for one bundle of ten. A drawing of a long stick can stand for a bundle, and a dot can stand for one. For 24, draw two ten-sticks and four dots: 20 and 4 together make twenty-four.

The left digit of a two-digit number counts tens; the right digit counts ones. A zero can hold a place: 60 has six tens and no extra ones. Ten tens make 100, called one hundred. Never count a ten-bundle as only one object when finding its value.

examples.prompt: A tray has 3 bundles of ten straws and 2 loose straws. How many straws?
steps: Each bundle stands for ten straws.
Three tens are 10, 20, 30.
Count two more: 31, 32; write 32.

examples.prompt: Make 70 with tens and ones.
steps: Read the 7 in the tens place.
Seven groups of ten make seventy.
The 0 shows that there are no loose ones.

explanation: To compare collections, first match objects one to one. If one collection has objects left over, it has more. For larger collections, compare their ten-bundles first. Four tens are more than three tens, even when the three tens have several loose ones.

If the tens are equal, compare the ones. In 52 and 57, both have five tens, but seven ones are more than two ones, so 57 is greater. Use the words greater than, less than, or equal to. A number line places smaller numbers to the left.

Ordering means arranging all given numbers, not just naming the largest. For smallest to greatest, select the fewest tens, then use ones to settle ties. Read 100 as ten tens; it comes after 99. Reversing the digits can change the value, so 26 and 62 are not equal.

examples.prompt: Which is greater: 46 or 39?
steps: 46 has four tens; 39 has three tens.
Four tens already exceed three tens and nine ones.
Therefore 46 is greater than 39.

examples.prompt: Order 72, 27 and 75 from smallest to greatest.
steps: 27 has two tens, so it is smallest.
72 and 75 each have seven tens.
Two ones are fewer than five ones, so 72 comes before 75.

items.prompt: Which is smaller, 41 or 14?

One ten and four ones is less than four tens and one one.

items.prompt: Put 20, 40 and 10 in increasing order.
steps: Increasing order starts with the smallest.
One ten, two tens, four tens gives 10, 20, 40.

items.prompt: Two piles each contain 6 tens and 2 ones. Compare their totals.
steps: Each pile has the same tens.
Each also has the same ones, so neither is greater.

items.prompt: On a number line, does 35 lie left or right of 38?
steps: 35 is less than 38 because 5 ones are fewer than 8.
Smaller numbers lie to the left.

explanation: A count answers how many; a position answers which place. In a row of five children, fifth describes one child’s place while five describes the whole group. Ordinal names are first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth and tenth.

Always identify the starting end. A row may be read from left to right, from right to left, or from the front of a queue. Mark the starting end and touch each object in order. The same object can have different positions when the direction changes.

Adding or removing someone before an object changes its position even though the object itself stays the same. Draw small boxes with names inside to keep track. Do not confuse a label printed on an object with its place; ticket 9 can be first in line.

examples.prompt: From left to right the cards are red, blue, green, yellow. Which card is third from the left?
steps: Start at the left as instructed.
Red is first and blue is second.
Green is third.

examples.prompt: From the front, a queue is Ali, Bea, Chen, Devi, Ean. What is Bea’s position from the back?
steps: Start at the back, with Ean.
Count Ean first, Devi second, Chen third.
Bea is fourth from the back.

steps: Count from A at the front.
The sixth name is F.

items.prompt: From left: sun, moon, star, cloud. What place is sun?
steps: Begin at the left.
Sun is the first object encountered.

items.prompt: Ten blocks stand in a row. Does tenth describe a total or a position?
steps: Ten is the total count.

items.prompt: From left: P, Q, R, S, T. Which is fourth?
steps: P, Q and R occupy the first three places.

items.prompt: Write the ordinal word for place 8.
steps: The count eight corresponds to place eight.
Its position word is eighth.

steps: G is at the right end.

items.prompt: A shelf has exactly 9 books. Can any book be tenth from the left?
steps: The positions run from first through ninth.
A tenth position would need a tenth book.

steps: Counting all ten from the front reaches Hana tenth.

weeks.objective: Recognise and extend increasing and decreasing patterns within 100.

connection.before: Read and order tens and ones; count positions.

Day 4: Choose worksheet B for independent representation and reasoning. Explain an answer aloud before checking the key.

explanation: A number pattern follows a stated or observed rule. In 12, 13, 14, 15, each next number is one more. In 20, 30, 40, each is ten more. Move counters or ten-bundles to show what changes, then record the numbers.

To fill a missing term, examine both neighbours and keep the same rule. In 31, 33, __, 37, the step is two, so 35 fits. A backward pattern removes the same amount each time. Saying the rule matters because a short list alone can have many possible continuations.

Crossing a ten changes the written digits. After 29 comes 30, because ten ones become a new ten. When counting back from 40 by ones, the next number is 39. We use only whole numbers from 0 to 100 in these paths; stop before the rule would leave that range.

examples.prompt: Count on by ones: 47, 48, __, __.
steps: The rule adds one each time.
One after 48 is 49.
One after 49 is 50, a new ten.

examples.prompt: Count back by tens: 86, 76, __, __.
steps: The ones digit stays 6.
Remove one ten from 76 to get 66.
Remove another ten to get 56.

steps: One after seven is eight.

items.prompt: Continue by tens: 10, 20, 30, __.
steps: Each step adds one ten.
One ten after thirty is forty.

items.prompt: Count back by ones: 15, 14, __, 12.
steps: One less than fourteen is thirteen.
Thirteen is one more than twelve.

items.prompt: Continue by twos: 2, 4, 6, __, __.
steps: Add two after six to reach eight.
Add two after eight to reach ten.

items.prompt: Say the rule: 25, 35, 45, 55.
steps: The ones stay five.
The tens increase by one bundle each step.

items.prompt: Write the number just before 60.
steps: Count backward one from sixty.
Exchange one ten for ones to see fifty-nine.

items.prompt: The rule is add one: 97, __, 99, __.

items.prompt: Count backward by tens: 70, 60, __, __.

Five tens minus one ten is four tens.

items.prompt: Which does not fit a count by twos: 11, 13, 16, 17? Repair it.

Two after 15 is 17, so the repaired path fits.

items.prompt: Start at 42 and make three jumps of ten forward. Where do you land?
steps: The landing numbers are 52, 62, 72.
Three jumps add three tens.

items.prompt: Start at 28. What is two steps later when counting by ones?
steps: The first step reaches 29.
The second step reaches 30.

steps: The stated rule adds two to the previous floor.

items.prompt: A child writes 38, 39, 310 when counting by ones. Correct the last number.

items.prompt: Give three numbers starting at 64 and counting back by ones. Include 64.
steps: 64 is the first number, not a jump.
Take one away twice to obtain 63 and 62.

items.prompt: Two paths start at 20. One adds ten; one adds one. Give their next numbers.
steps: Adding a ten changes two tens to three tens.
Adding one leaves two tens and adds a single one.

items.prompt: Choose a starting number so counting by fives gives __, 40, 45.
steps: The missing number must be five less than 40.
35, 40, 45 has equal jumps of five.

items.prompt: A path counts back by twos from 8 to 0. Write the full path.
steps: Remove two at each step.
Stop at zero so the path stays within whole numbers to 100.

weeks.title: Joining parts within twenty
weeks.objective: Represent addition as joining two parts to make a whole.

connection.before: Count on and recognise a whole collection.
connection.after: Subtract by separating a part from a whole.

days: Day 1: An adult reads directions as needed. Explore joining parts within twenty with counters, a quick sketch, or the fully described model. Say what each part represents.
Day 2: Read the explanation and work through both examples. Cover the answer, predict it, then explain each step.
Day 3: Choose worksheet A for supported practice. Match the objects or pictured groups to the written numbers.
Day 4: Choose worksheet B for independent representation and reasoning. Explain an answer aloud before checking the key.
Day 5: Choose worksheet C for applications and error checking. Revisit a difficult item using a different representation.
explanation: Addition joins quantities. Put one group of counters beside another without counting any counter twice. A number bond names the two parts and their whole. A text bar such as [4][3] has parts four and three and a whole of seven.

The symbol + means add, and = means the amounts on both sides have the same value. For a joining story, write first part + second part = whole. You can count all the counters, or keep the larger part in mind and count on the smaller part.

The order of the two parts does not change the whole: red counters joined to blue counters give the same total when their positions are swapped. Adding zero changes nothing. Read the question carefully: the whole includes both parts, not only the new objects.

examples.prompt: A pond has 6 ducks. 3 ducks join them. How many ducks now?
steps: Show six counters for the ducks already there.
Add three counters and count on 7, 8, 9.
Write 6 + 3 = 9 ducks.

examples.prompt: A bar has parts 8 and 5. Find its whole.
steps: The bar joins both parts.
Count on five from eight: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13.
The whole is 13, so 8 + 5 = 13.

steps: Check by taking 1 from 8: 8 − 1 = 7.

steps: Check by taking 0 from 9: 9 − 0 = 9.

items.prompt: Write the two parts of the whole in 2 + 6 = 8.
steps: The numbers being added are the parts.
8 is the whole made by joining them.

steps: Check by taking 5 from 16: 16 − 5 = 11.

items.prompt: There are 8 large buttons and 8 small buttons. How many buttons altogether?
steps: Check by taking 8 from 16: 16 − 8 = 8.

items.prompt: A class sees 12 butterflies, then 2 more. Find the total.
steps: Check by taking 2 from 14: 14 − 2 = 12.

items.prompt: Is 0 + 15 equal to 15 + 0? Explain.

items.answer: The original 5 balls were left out; there are 7 now.

Five and two together make seven.

items.answer: For example, 4 and 6; any unequal positive pair totaling 10 works.
steps: Draw ten counters and split them into two unequal nonempty groups.
Four counters and six counters together still make ten.

explanation: Subtraction removes a part from a whole. First draw the whole as tens and ones. If it has enough loose ones, remove the ones and then the tens. For 57 − 23, remove three ones and two tens, leaving three tens and four ones.

explanation: Equal groups contain the same number in every group. Count the groups, then count objects in one group. Three bowls with four counters each have the repeated parts 4 + 4 + 4. Unequal bowls do not fit one repeated equal part.

explanation: An array is a rectangular arrangement with the same number of objects in each row. A row runs across; a column runs down. Count the rows and then the objects in one row to describe the array as equal groups.

You can also count the columns and the objects in one column. A rectangle with two rows of five dots is also five columns of two dots. Both count the same ten dots once, so 2 × 5 and 5 × 2 have the same total, though their group descriptions differ.

explanation: Sharing starts with a whole collection and a known number of groups. Give one object to each group in turn, then repeat. Stop when the whole collection is used. Fair shares contain the same number of objects.

The division symbol ÷ records a split into equal parts. Here 12 ÷ 3 means share twelve among three groups and find how many go in each. Draw three circles and distribute twelve dots; four dots end in each circle.

Check both fairness and the whole. Equal-sized groups are not enough if some objects were forgotten or added. Add the shares to recover the starting total. These tasks use whole objects and exact shares; if an exact whole-object share is impossible, say so rather than quietly dropping leftovers.

examples.prompt: Share 15 counters equally among 5 children. How many each?

Deal one counter into each space for three rounds, using all fifteen.
Each gets three; five groups of three rebuild fifteen.

examples.prompt: Share 8 cubes equally between 2 boxes. How many in each?

explanation: Grouping starts with a whole and a known size for each group. To pack twelve objects three per bag, circle three objects at a time and count the bags. The unknown is how many groups, not how many objects go in each.

The equation 12 ÷ 3 = 4 can describe four groups of three or three groups of four, depending on what the divisor means in the story. Label the model with the words bags, children, or objects each. An equation alone does not name those roles.

Multiplication checks a grouping result: number of groups × size of each group gives the whole. The grouping and sharing totals here stay within twenty; multiplication representations stay within forty. Use counters rather than assuming memorised tables.

explanation: A centimetre, written cm, is a length unit. Imagine a ruler with equally spaced marks labelled 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on; every gap between neighbouring marks is one centimetre. Length counts the gaps covered, not the printed marks.

Place one end of an object at the zero mark and keep the ruler straight along it. Read the mark at the other end. An object from 0 to 7 measures 7 cm. If its first end is not at zero, count the intervening gaps or subtract the starting reading from the ending reading.

For the nearest centimetre, choose the whole-centimetre mark closer to the endpoint. These tasks avoid endpoints exactly halfway between marks. Label the answer cm. The ruler’s physical edge may lie before zero, so lining up with the edge is not always correct.

examples.prompt: A ribbon begins at 0 cm and ends at 9 cm on a ruler. Find its length.
steps: The zero mark is the starting point.
Count nine one-centimetre intervals to the endpoint.
Write 9 cm, including the length unit.

examples.prompt: A pencil begins at 3 cm and ends at 11 cm. Find its length.
steps: The pencil does not begin at zero.
Count the gaps from 3 to 11, or find 11 − 3.
There are eight gaps, so the length is 8 cm.

Five one-centimetre gaps reach mark five.

steps: The zero start means the endpoint reading gives the length.
The segment covers twelve centimetre intervals.

items.prompt: A bead chain spans four equal 1 cm gaps. How long is it?
steps: Each of the four gaps contributes one centimetre.
Four one-centimetre units make four centimetres.

items.prompt: On a ruler, marks 0, 1, 2, 3 are visible. How many 1 cm gaps lie from 0 to 3?

Four marks bound three gaps.

items.prompt: A child places a strip at the ruler’s edge, which is before 0. What should be changed?
items.answer: Move the strip’s start to the 0 mark.
steps: The edge is not the measurement origin in this ruler.
Using zero makes the endpoint reading the length.

items.prompt: Which label is suitable for a pencil length: 8 cm or 8 counters?

Centimetres measure length; counters name objects.

Unequal gaps would assign different lengths to the same unit.

The endpoint is stated to be nearer fourteen.

explanation: To draw a segment of a given length, mark its starting point at zero on a ruler. Mark the required centimetre endpoint and join the two marks with a straight line. When a real ruler is unavailable, a described unit strip or equally spaced centimetre marks can show the same plan.

For direct comparison, line up one end of two strips. The one reaching farther is longer. If numerical lengths are given in the same unit, compare the numbers; subtract shorter from longer to find the extra length. Label both lengths and the difference cm.

Joining strips end to end adds their lengths only if there is no gap or overlap. A gap adds space that is not part of either strip, and overlap counts some length twice. Draw the endpoints and say the arrangement before choosing an addition sentence.

Starting at two, count seven gaps forward.

explanation: A plane shape is a flat figure with a boundary. A triangle has three straight sides and three corners. A square has four equal straight sides and four square corners. A rectangle has four straight sides and four square corners, with opposite sides equal.

A circle has a curved boundary and no corners. Turning or sliding a shape does not change its kind. A square balanced on a corner is still a square. Look at the sides and corners rather than whether the figure resembles a familiar object.

A square also meets the rectangle description, so a square can correctly be called a special rectangle. When asked for the most specific name, use square. These are flat shapes; the outline of a box face can be a rectangle, but the whole solid box is not a flat rectangle.

examples.prompt: A flat figure has three straight sides and three corners. Name it.
steps: Count its three boundary sides.
The three sides join at three corners.
These properties identify a triangle, regardless of its direction.

examples.prompt: A square is turned so one corner points up. What is its name now?
steps: Turning changes its position, not its side lengths.
Its four equal sides and four square corners remain.
It is still a square, also a special rectangle.

explanation: A half-circle is one of two matching pieces made by a straight cut through the centre of a circle. Its boundary has one straight edge and one curved edge. A quarter-circle is one of four matching pieces made by two crossing cuts through the centre at a square corner.

Two matching half-circles can reassemble the original circle when their straight edges meet. Four matching quarter-circles can also make that circle. The pieces must come from the same-size circle for these constructions; names alone do not guarantee matching sizes.

Composition joins pieces into a larger figure. Describe both the pieces and the outside boundary. A line where pieces meet lies inside the completed figure, so it need not be counted as an outside edge. Turning a piece changes its orientation but does not change which piece it is.

explanation: A construction plan tells another person what to draw or place. Give the shape names, lengths that matter, and relative positions such as above, beside or sharing an edge. A text plan can be tested with a labelled sketch; it need not depend on an unseen picture.

When shapes join, count pieces separately from the completed figure. Two squares of side 3 cm placed side by side create a rectangle 6 cm wide and 3 cm high. The shared side is internal. This uses simple length addition, not an area or perimeter formula.

Check a plan against each condition: equal lengths must match, circular pieces must have the stated sizes, and joins must leave no gaps or overlaps. If several drawings meet the instructions, more than one answer can be correct. Explain the features that make yours fit.

explanation: A clock face has the numbers 1 to 12 arranged around a circle. The longer hand is the minute hand; the shorter hand is the hour hand. When the minute hand points to 12, the clock shows an exact hour and the hour hand points to that hour’s number.

One complete journey of the minute hand takes one hour, or sixty minutes. Halfway round it reaches 6 after thirty minutes. The hour hand also moves: at half past an hour it lies halfway between that hour and the next.

To read half past, name the hour already passed, not the next hour. If the short hand is halfway between 4 and 5 and the long hand is at 6, the time is half past four, written 4:30. A clock drawing alone does not tell whether it is morning or afternoon.

examples.prompt: The minute hand points to 12 and the hour hand points to 7. What time is shown?

First find the minute reading, then identify the hour already passed. At 3:45, the minute hand is at 9 and the hour hand is between 3 and 4, nearer 4. Even when the hour hand is close to the next number, the named hour remains three until it reaches four.

The two hands use the same numbered marks differently. A long hand at 4 means twenty minutes, not four minutes. Written times put the hour before the colon and minutes after it; use two minute digits, such as :05. These lessons read time only in five-minute steps.

explanation: A clock face repeats its readings twice each day. The label am covers midnight up to before noon, and pm covers noon up to before the next midnight. For a typical daily story, morning times such as 8:00 am come before afternoon times such as 3:00 pm.

Twelve needs special care: 12:00 pm is noon and 12:00 am is midnight. After 11:55 am comes noon at 12:00 pm; after 12:55 pm comes 1:00 pm. Use a supplied daily context, not only a guess about when an activity usually happens.

To order a day’s events, first identify their am or pm part of the day, then read hours and minutes. Within the same hour, compare minutes. These tasks explicitly refer to one day unless stated otherwise, so do not accidentally put an evening event before a morning event because its hour numeral is smaller.

explanation: Duration tells how much time passes between a start and an end. An hour is sixty minutes; half an hour is thirty minutes. On a clock, one hour moves the minute hand one full turn, while half an hour moves it half a turn.

One hour later has the same minute reading and the next hour number. Half an hour later moves the minute hand six numbered steps. If this passes the 12 mark, the hour increases. For example, half an hour after 2:40 is 3:10.

Check by moving back the same amount. Include am or pm when supplied and change the label at noon. Our duration problems use only half an hour or one hour; they do not require unrestricted elapsed-time calculation. A drawing can trace the hand movement in five-minute steps.

examples.prompt: A game starts at 9:20 am and lasts one hour. When does it end?

The minute reading remains twenty.
The hour advances from nine to ten, giving 10:20 am.

examples.prompt: A story starts at 11:45 am and lasts half an hour. When does it end?

explanation: A coin has a stated value. Count value, not just how many coins are present: a 20-cent coin contributes twenty cents while a 5-cent coin contributes five. In these pretend collections every denomination is explicitly named, so no coin picture is needed.

Group like coins or start with the greatest value and count on. For 20 cents, 10 cents and 5 cents, say twenty, thirty, thirty-five cents. Write cents or the symbol ¢ consistently. One hundred cents has the same value as one dollar.

Keep units clear. A collection of three coins need not have a value of three cents. We count amounts up to 100 cents and do not use decimal dollar notation in this Primary 1 work. All coin sets in a question are complete; do not assume unseen coins.

explanation: Different collections can have equal total value. Two 10-cent coins can replace one 20-cent coin. The exchange changes the number of coins but keeps the amount of money. Use drawn circles with their cent values written inside.

To build a target, choose a useful coin and work out the remaining amount. For a target of 35 cents, a 20-cent coin leaves 15 cents, which can be made by 10 and 5. Check the completed set by adding every coin value.

A question may limit the allowed coins or the number of coins. Follow all those conditions; there may be several valid answers or none. When asked for fewer coins, compare coin counts only after checking that the values are equal. Never assume the largest number of coins has the greatest value.

explanation: The dollar sign $ names a dollar amount. In this week $27 means twenty-seven whole dollars. We keep dollars separate from cents and do not introduce decimal notation. One $10 value marker is ten dollars, regardless of whether it is drawn as a coin, note or labelled card.

Group $10 markers as tens and $1 markers as ones. Other supplied values such as $2, $5 and $50 can be combined by addition. Count the values written on the markers, not their size or colour. All amounts in these tasks are stated explicitly.

The 4 in four represents four ones, so the place changes the value.

items.prompt: Give two different sets of supplied $1, $2, $5 and $10 markers worth $12.

Both examples use only allowed values and preserve the same amount.

explanation: A price tells how much an item costs. Joining the prices of two items gives their total cost. Keep the money unit the same throughout a question: add cent prices to cent prices, or whole-dollar prices to whole-dollar prices.

Change is the money returned when the payment is greater than the cost. A bar shows payment as the whole, with cost and change as its two parts. Subtract cost from payment or count on from cost to payment. Paying exactly the price gives zero change.

Check a change answer by adding it to the cost. The result must equal the payment. If the price is greater than the money available, the question is about how much more is needed, not change received. These pretend prices supply every fact needed.

examples.prompt: A card costs 35 cents. You pay 50 cents. Find the change.
steps: The fifty-cent payment is the whole.
Subtract the cost: 50 − 35 = 15 cents.
Check 35 + 15 = 50 cents.

examples.prompt: A book costs $12 and a bag costs $8. Find their total price.
steps: Both prices are in whole dollars.
Join the two cost parts: 12 + 8 = 20.
Subtracting either price from twenty recovers the other.

items.prompt: A pencil costs 20 cents and an eraser 15 cents. Find the total cost.

items.prompt: A cup costs $4 and a plate $9. Find the total price.

items.prompt: An item costs 50 cents and the buyer pays 50 cents. How much change?

There is no extra amount to return.

items.prompt: A child adds 30 and 50 to find change from a 50-cent payment for a 30-cent item. Correct it.

50 − 30 = 20; cost plus change returns fifty.

items.prompt: A $13 purchase and $7 change come from what payment?

Fifteen covers fourteen and leaves one dollar.

explanation: A money comparison puts two amounts beside each other. Draw bars starting at the same point and label both with cents or both with dollars. The extra part of the longer bar is the difference. Subtract the smaller amount from the larger.

When one amount and the difference are given, rebuild the missing amount. If a bag costs $6 more than a $15 cap, add the extra six to the known fifteen. If an item costs $6 less than the cap, remove six. The direction matters.

Check what the question asks: total cost, difference, amount needed or money remaining. All are possible even with similar numbers. An answer in dollars cannot be silently compared with an answer in cents. Use a supplied story and a labelled bar to justify each operation.

examples.prompt: A red notebook costs 75 cents; a blue one costs 50 cents. How much cheaper is blue?
steps: Align bars of seventy-five and fifty cents.
Remove the matching fifty from seventy-five.
The extra twenty-five means blue costs 25 cents less.

examples.prompt: Lena saves $28. Max saves $9 less. How much has Max saved?
steps: Max’s bar is shorter than Lena’s by nine dollars.
Subtract 28 − 9 = 19.
Check that 19 + 9 = 28, matching the comparison.

steps: Put the parts back together: 15 + 25 = 40.

items.prompt: A pen costs $3. A notebook costs $4 more. Find the notebook price.

items.prompt: A bag costs $18. A cap costs $5 less. Find the cap price.
steps: Put the parts back together: 13 + 5 = 18.

items.prompt: Two toy prices are both $12. What is the difference?

12 − 12 = 0 dollars.

items.prompt: A learner adds 20 cents and 35 cents to find their difference. Correct it.
steps: The sum would give the joined total, not the gap.

steps: Put the parts back together: 35 + 55 = 90.

Jo’s extra seven makes twenty-seven and gives the difference.

Remove the extra six: 16 − 6 = 10.

steps: Check by taking 20 from 85: 85 − 20 = 65.

items.prompt: An item costs $31, which is $12 more than a second item. Find the second price.
steps: Put the parts back together: 19 + 12 = 31.

items.prompt: A child says “5 dollars is less than 20 cents because 5 is less than 20.” Explain.
items.answer: The units differ; 5 dollars is greater.
steps: One dollar alone equals one hundred cents, already more than twenty cents.
Five dollars therefore exceeds twenty cents; compare values with attention to units.

items.prompt: Choose two different whole-dollar prices at most $20 whose difference is $7.
steps: Choose a smaller price such as eight dollars.
Add seven to get fifteen; both satisfy the limit.

items.prompt: A buyer has $30. A book costs $12 and a bag costs $15. Find the total cost and money left.
steps: 12 + 15 = 27 dollars joins the prices.
30 − 27 = 3 dollars checks the spending plan.

weeks.objective: Read categories, keys and counts in unscaled picture graphs.

connection.before: Count whole numbers and compare amounts.
connection.after: Use picture-graph counts to find totals and differences.

days: Day 1: An adult reads directions as needed. Explore read one-picture-one-object graphs with counters, a quick sketch, or the fully described model. Say what each part represents.
Day 2: Read the explanation and work through both examples. Cover the answer, predict it, then explain each step.
Day 3: Choose worksheet A for supported practice. Match the objects or pictured groups to the written numbers.
Day 4: Choose worksheet B for independent representation and reasoning. Explain an answer aloud before checking the key.
Day 5: Choose worksheet C for applications and error checking. Revisit a difficult item using a different representation.
explanation: A picture graph records counts in labelled rows. Its key tells what each picture represents. In this unit every full picture stands for exactly one object or one vote. For example, “Pens: ● ● ●” with key “● = one pen” shows three pens.

Read the category label before counting its pictures. Pictures are records, not decoration; count each once. An empty row records zero when the category is included. The number of categories is different from the total number of objects represented.

Align equal-size pictures when drawing a graph so comparisons are easy. Wide spacing must not make a row seem to contain more objects. Count pictures or use one-to-one matching to compare. We do not use scaled pictures worth two or more objects in Primary 1.

examples.prompt: Picture graph, key ● = 1 vote: Red: ● ● ●; Blue: ● ● ● ● ●. How many votes for Blue?
steps: Read the Blue category label.
Count its five pictures, each worth one vote.
The graph records five Blue votes.

examples.prompt: Key ★ = 1 kite: Plain: ★ ★; Striped: no pictures. How many striped kites?
steps: Find the Striped row.
There are no pictures in that row.
With one picture per kite, no pictures means zero kites.

worksheets.directions: An adult may read all text aloud. Draw or use counters when helpful; all needed quantities are supplied. Explain your thinking in words, drawings, or number sentences. Work on a few tasks at a time. Point to a model or answer aloud if writing is a barrier; an adult may record the response.

items.prompt: Key ● = 1 apple. Green: ● ●; Red: ● ● ● ●. How many green apples?
steps: Use the row labelled Green.
Its two pictures each represent one apple.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 book. Fiction: ★ ★ ★; Facts: ★ ★. How many fiction books?
steps: Find Fiction, not Facts.
Three stars mean three books.

items.prompt: Key ■ = 1 cup. Blue: ■ ■ ■ ■ ■; Yellow: ■. How many yellow cups?
steps: The Yellow row has one square.
One square represents one cup.

items.prompt: Key ● = 1 vote. Cat: ● ● ●; Dog: ● ●; Fish: ●. How many categories?
steps: Read the labels Cat, Dog and Fish.
There are three categories, not six categories.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 seed. Tray A: ★ ★; Tray B: no stars. What does Tray B show?
steps: The included category has an empty picture row.
No stars means no recorded seeds.

items.prompt: A graph uses key ● = 1 child. A row has four ● pictures. Does it show four children or four groups of ten?
steps: The key assigns one child to each picture.
Four pictures therefore represent four children.

worksheets.title: Connect and reason: Read one-picture-one-object graphs
worksheets.directions: An adult may read all text aloud. Draw or use counters when helpful; all needed quantities are supplied. Explain your thinking in words, drawings, or number sentences. Work on a few tasks at a time. Point to a model or answer aloud if writing is a barrier; an adult may record the response.

items.prompt: Key ■ = 1 toy. Cars: ■ ■ ■ ■; Boats: ■ ■; Trains: ■ ■ ■. Which category has most?
steps: Count four cars, two boats and three trains.
Four is the greatest count.

items.prompt: Key ● = 1 fruit. Pears: ● ● ●; Plums: ●; Peaches: ● ●. Which has fewest?
steps: The counts are three, one and two.
One is the smallest count.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 sticker. A: ★ ★ ★; B: ★ ★ ★. Compare A and B.
steps: Count three stars in both rows.
Matching each star leaves none unmatched.

items.prompt: Key ■ = 1 bead. Red: ■ ■; Blue: ■ ■ ■ ■ ■. A child says blue has 6 because there are 2 labels. Correct the count.
steps: Labels name rows and are not bead pictures.
Count only the five squares in Blue.

items.prompt: Key ● = 1 basket. Full: ● ● ● ●; Empty: ● ●. How many baskets are recorded altogether?
steps: The categories both record baskets.
Four full plus two empty equals six baskets.

items.prompt: A graph key says ★ = 1 shell. One row spaces its three stars far apart. Another puts three stars close together. Which has more shells?
steps: Spacing does not change the picture count.
Each row has three one-shell pictures.

worksheets.title: Use and check: Read one-picture-one-object graphs
worksheets.directions: An adult may read all text aloud. Draw or use counters when helpful; all needed quantities are supplied. Explain your thinking in words, drawings, or number sentences. Work on a few tasks at a time. Point to a model or answer aloud if writing is a barrier; an adult may record the response.

items.prompt: Key ■ = 1 vote. Walk: ■ ■ ■ ■; Dance: ■ ■; Sing: ■ ■ ■. How many votes for Sing?
steps: Find the Sing row.
Count its three one-vote pictures.

items.prompt: Key ● = 1 packet. Seeds: ● ● ● ● ● ●; Beads: ● ●. A child says there are 2 packets because there are 2 rows. Find the total.
steps: Rows count kinds of packets, not individual packets.
Six seed packets plus two bead packets gives eight.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 marble. Red: ★ ★; Blue: ★ ★ ★. What label belongs to the row with three stars?
steps: Match the described row to the supplied graph.
The Blue row contains exactly three stars.

items.prompt: Key ■ = 1 hat. Caps: ■ ■ ■; Sunhats: ■. Give one true statement about the graph.
items.answer: For example, there are 3 caps or caps outnumber sunhats.
steps: Use the shown counts, three and one.
Any statement supported by those counts is acceptable.

items.prompt: A drawing has five dots with no key or category label. Can you know whether they represent five books or five votes?
steps: Counting yields five pictures.
The missing label and key prevent knowing what the pictures represent.

items.prompt: Key ● = 1 pencil. Short: ● ● ● ●; Long: ● ●. Which claim fits: “long has most” or “short has most”?
steps: Short has four pictures, while Long has two.
Four is more than two.

explanation: Read the graph’s key and count the needed rows before calculating. A question about two categories together joins their counts. A question asking how many more compares them by subtracting the smaller count from the larger.

You can see a difference by matching pictures across two aligned rows. The pictures left unmatched in the longer row show how many more. Turn that picture comparison into a labelled equation, such as 7 − 4 = 3 votes.

Include only the categories named by the question. If a graph has three rows and asks for two together, adding the third changes the question. A graph describes its recorded group; it does not prove what everyone outside that group prefers.

examples.prompt: Key ● = 1 vote. Art: ● ● ● ● ● ●; Music: ● ● ● ●. How many more votes for Art?
steps: Count six for Art and four for Music.
Match four pictures; Art has two left unmatched.
6 − 4 = 2 votes is the difference.

examples.prompt: Key ★ = 1 box. Small: ★ ★; Medium: ★ ★ ★; Large: ★ ★ ★ ★. How many small and large boxes together?
steps: Select Small and Large only.
Their counts are two and four.
2 + 4 = 6; leave out the medium boxes.

worksheets.directions: An adult may read all text aloud. Draw or use counters when helpful; all needed quantities are supplied. Explain your thinking in words, drawings, or number sentences. Work on a few tasks at a time. Point to a model or answer aloud if writing is a barrier; an adult may record the response.

items.prompt: Key ● = 1 vote. Red: ● ● ● ● ●; Green: ● ●. How many more Red votes?
steps: The counts are five and two.
5 − 2 = 3 unmatched votes.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 flower. Roses: ★ ★ ★; Lilies: ★ ★ ★ ★. Find their total.
steps: Read three roses and four lilies.
3 + 4 = 7 flowers.

items.prompt: Key ■ = 1 toy. Cars: ■ ■ ■ ■ ■ ■; Boats: ■ ■ ■ ■. How many fewer boats?
steps: Compare the six cars with four boats.
6 − 4 = 2, so there are two fewer boats.

items.prompt: Key ● = 1 book. A: ● ●; B: ● ● ●; C: ● ● ● ●. Find A and B together.
steps: Select only rows A and B.
2 + 3 = 5 books.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 fruit. Apples: ★ ★ ★; Pears: ★ ★ ★. Find the difference.
steps: Each row has three fruits.
3 − 3 = 0; no pictures are unmatched.

items.prompt: Key ■ = 1 cup. Red: ■ ■ ■ ■; Blue: ■ ■. A learner says “2 more red” by adding. Correct the explanation.
steps: The answer two describes an unmatched part.
Adding would give six cups altogether, a different question.

worksheets.directions: An adult may read all text aloud. Draw or use counters when helpful; all needed quantities are supplied. Explain your thinking in words, drawings, or number sentences. items.prompt: Key ● = 1 child. Chess: ● ● ● ● ● ● ●; Art: ● ● ● ●; Music: ● ● ●. How many choose Art or Music?
steps: Art has four and Music has three.
4 + 3 = 7 children in those two categories.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 pencil. Short: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ ★; Long: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★. How many more short pencils?
steps: The counts are eight and five.
8 − 5 = 3 gives the difference.

items.prompt: Key ■ = 1 shell. White: ■ ■ ■ ■ ■; Brown: ■ ■ ■; Grey: ■ ■. How many shells altogether?
steps: The three counts are five, three and two.
Pair three and two to make five; five plus five is ten.

items.prompt: Key ● = 1 badge. Gold: ● ● ● ● ● ●; Silver: ● ● ● ● ● ●. How many more gold badges?
steps: Both rows show six badges.
Equal counts have a difference of zero.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 vote. Tea: ★ ★; Milk: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★; Water: ★ ★ ★. Which two categories total 5 votes?
steps: Tea has two and Water has three.
Two plus three is five; the other pairs exceed five.

items.prompt: Key ■ = 1 marker. Black: ■ ■ ■ ■ ■ ■ ■; Green: ■ ■ ■. How many green markers must be added to tie?
steps: Seven black markers must be matched.
7 − 3 = 4 more green markers are needed.

worksheets.directions: An adult may read all text aloud. Draw or use counters when helpful; all needed quantities are supplied. Explain your thinking in words, drawings, or number sentences. Work on a few tasks at a time. Point to a model or answer aloud if writing is a barrier; an adult may record the response.

items.prompt: Key ● = 1 vote. Drawing: ● ● ● ● ● ●; Singing: ● ● ●; Reading: ● ●. How many votes for all three?
steps: The row counts are six, three and two.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 toy. Planes: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★; Boats: ★ ★; Cars: ★ ★ ★ ★. How many more planes than boats?
steps: Read five planes and two boats.
5 − 2 = 3; the car count is not needed.

items.prompt: Key ■ = 1 child. Ball game: ■ ■ ■ ■; Board game: ■ ■ ■. Is it proven that every child in the country prefers ball games?
steps: The graph records only seven children’s choices.
Four versus three in this group does not establish everyone’s preference.

items.prompt: Key ● = 1 packet. Red: ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ●; Blue: ● ● ● ●. A child says red is 12 more. Correct the statement.
items.answer: Red is 4 more; 12 is the total

Eight minus four gives the difference four.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 ribbon. Yellow: ★ ★; Purple: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ ★. State both the total and the difference.
steps: 2 + 6 = 8 joins the rows.
6 − 2 = 4 compares them.

items.prompt: Key ■ = 1 vote. A: ■ ■ ■ ■ ■; B: ■ ■ ■; C: ■. Can A’s 5 votes equal B and C together?
steps: Three plus one is four.
Five is one greater than four.

connection.before: Read and compare picture graph counts.

days: Day 1: An adult reads directions as needed. Explore make and revise a picture graph with counters, a quick sketch, or the fully described model. Say what each part represents.
Day 2: Read the explanation and work through both examples. Cover the answer, predict it, then explain each step.

Day 4: Choose worksheet B for independent representation and reasoning. Explain an answer aloud before checking the key.

explanation: To make a picture graph, choose categories and a key of one picture for one object. Count the supplied records into the categories. Draw one equal-size picture for each record and label every row. Keep an empty row when a listed category has zero.

Check the total number of graph pictures against the original records. Each record belongs once in the stated category; do not count one record twice or skip it. This check can catch a graph that looks tidy but records the wrong information.

When the data change, change only the affected rows. An added object needs one new picture; a removed object needs one picture removed. A correction that moves one record between categories changes both rows but preserves the grand total. The key remains one picture per object.

examples.prompt: Records of pet choices: cat, dog, cat, bird, cat, dog. Make a graph with ● = 1 vote.
steps: Sort the six records by their stated categories.
Count three cats, two dogs and one bird.
Draw six pictures in total and check 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

examples.prompt: Key ★ = 1 book. Story: ★ ★; Facts: ★ ★ ★. One facts book was actually a storybook. Correct the graph.
steps: Remove one picture from Facts.
Add that picture to Story.
The total remains five books: 3 + 2 = 5.

worksheets.directions: An adult may read all text aloud. Draw or use counters when helpful; all needed quantities are supplied. Explain your thinking in words, drawings, or number sentences. items.prompt: Data: 4 red cups and 2 blue cups. Write a graph using ● = 1 cup.
steps: Use one picture for each stated cup.
Check four plus two gives six pictures altogether.

items.prompt: List: apple, pear, apple, apple, pear. How many pictures go in each row with ★ = 1 fruit?
steps: Count each label once in the list.
Three apple and two pear pictures account for all five fruits.

items.prompt: Data: circles 2, squares 0, triangles 3. Describe a graph with ■ = 1 shape.
items.answer: Circles: 2 pictures; Squares: no pictures; Triangles: 3 pictures
steps: Keep all three named categories.
Zero squares means an empty row, while the total is five pictures.

items.prompt: A graph for 3 pencils shows four pencil pictures with key ● = 1 pencil. Repair it.
steps: The key requires one picture for each of three pencils.
Four pictures overcounts by one.

items.prompt: A graph has no key. All pictures are intended to mean one vote. Supply the missing key.
steps: The key states the unit value of each picture.
This makes each row count interpretable.

items.prompt: Data: 2 buses and 4 cars. A graph labels the four-picture row Buses. What must be fixed?
items.answer: Swap the row labels, or redraw so Buses has 2 and Cars has 4
steps: The category labels must match the supplied counts.
Both the numbers and their named categories need to agree.

Work on a few tasks at a time. Point to a model or answer aloud if writing is a barrier; an adult may record the response.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 flower. Pink: ★ ★ ★; White: ★ ★. Add 2 white flowers. Give new row counts.
steps: Pink does not change.
White grows from two to four; the new total is seven.

items.prompt: Key ● = 1 toy. Cars: ● ● ● ● ●; Boats: ● ● ●. Remove 2 cars. Give new counts.
steps: Five cars minus two leaves three.
The boat row remains three, so the rows now tie.

items.prompt: List: red, blue, green, red, green, red, blue. Build row counts for a one-vote picture graph.
steps: Tally each of the seven records once.
Three plus two plus two equals seven, checking the total.

items.prompt: Data say 6 yellow beads and 3 black beads. A graph shows Yellow 5 pictures, Black 4. Is matching total enough?
items.answer: No; move one picture from Black to Yellow
steps: Both totals are nine, but the category counts are wrong.
Six yellow and three black must be shown.

items.prompt: Key ■ = 1 child. A: ■ ■; B: ■ ■ ■ ■. One child switches from B to A. Give the new counts.
steps: A gains one picture and B loses one.
The whole remains six children.

items.prompt: A graph represents 8 objects with one picture per object. It currently has 3 pictures in one row and 4 in another. What is missing?
items.answer: 1 picture, but its category needs checking against the data
steps: The shown total is seven.
Eight minus seven is one; totals alone do not identify its row.

worksheets.directions: An adult may read all text aloud. Draw or use counters when helpful; all needed quantities are supplied. Explain your thinking in words, drawings, or number sentences. Work on a few tasks at a time. Point to a model or answer aloud if writing is a barrier; an adult may record the response.

items.prompt: Supplies list: glue, paper, paper, brush, glue, paper. Make a text graph using ● = 1 item.
steps: Count two glue items, three paper items and one brush.
The graph has six pictures matching the six records.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 vote. Art: ★ ★ ★ ★; Sport: ★ ★. Three new sport votes arrive. Which row is now greatest?
steps: Add three to the original two Sport votes.
Five Sport votes exceed the unchanged four Art votes.

items.prompt: A graph has 3 rows of 2, 5 and 4 pictures. Its key is one picture per packet. How many original packets should there be?
steps: Join the row counts two, five and four.
2 + 5 + 4 = 11 packets should match the records.

items.prompt: A survey lists 4 red choices and 4 blue choices. Draw one row with wide gaps and one with tight gaps. Should the row counts differ?
steps: Spacing is a layout choice, not a data value.
Use four equal-value pictures in each row to preserve the tie.

items.prompt: Invent counts for three categories with 9 objects altogether, including one empty category.
steps: The counts must be nonnegative whole numbers and one must be zero.
4 + 5 + 0 = 9 fits; draw that many one-object pictures.

items.prompt: A graph shows Red 3, Blue 2 and Green 1 with one picture per vote. Its title says “10 votes.” What needs checking?
items.answer: The title or missing records: only 6 votes are shown
steps: Add the category counts: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.
The total does not match ten, so consult the supplied records before adding arbitrary pictures.

weeks.title: A class supply plan
weeks.objective: Use graphs, number bonds and equal groups to make and check a simple class plan.

connection.before: Build accurate graphs and reason about equal groups and missing parts.
connection.after: Extend to hundreds, selected multiplication tables and scaled picture graphs in Primary 2.

days: Day 1: An adult reads directions as needed. Explore a class supply plan with counters, a quick sketch, or the fully described model. Say what each part represents.
Day 2: Read the explanation and work through both examples. Cover the answer, predict it, then explain each step.
Day 3: Choose worksheet A for supported practice. Match the objects or pictured groups to the written numbers.
Day 4: Choose worksheet B for independent representation and reasoning. Explain an answer aloud before checking the key.
Day 5: Choose worksheet C for applications and error checking. Revisit a difficult item using a different representation.
explanation: A useful plan begins with the available quantities and a clear target. Read the supplied graph or list, then decide whether the question needs a total, a difference, an equal share or a repeated-group total. Label a drawing so another person can follow the quantities.

For equal resource packs, every pack must receive the same number of each required item. Check both the number of packs and the items per pack. A supply of twelve pencils makes four packs of three pencils, but not four packs of four. Count leftovers separately when a plan explicitly allows them.

Explain why the plan works, not only what the answer is. Rebuild a shared total by adding the equal parts, compare the used amount with the supply, and check a graph against its key. These tasks stay in Primary 1 whole-number, equal-group and one-picture graph scope; an adult can record an oral explanation.

examples.prompt: Key ● = 1 pencil. Red: ● ● ● ● ● ●; Blue: ● ● ● ● ● ●. Share all pencils equally into 3 packs. How many per pack?
steps: The graph contains six red and six blue, twelve altogether.
Share twelve pencils among three packs: four in each.
3 × 4 = 12 checks that all pencils are used equally.

examples.prompt: Four craft packs each need 5 paper stars. The class has 16 stars. How many more are needed?
steps: Four equal groups of five need twenty stars.
Compare the target twenty with the available sixteen.
20 − 16 = 4 more stars; 16 + 4 checks the target.

worksheets.title: Build and describe: A class supply plan
worksheets.directions: An adult may read all text aloud. Draw or use counters when helpful; all needed quantities are supplied. Explain your thinking in words, drawings, or number sentences. Work on a few tasks at a time. Point to a model or answer aloud if writing is a barrier; an adult may record the response.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 brush. Thin: ★ ★ ★; Thick: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★. How many brushes are available?
steps: Count three thin and five thick brushes.
3 + 5 = 8 available brushes.

items.prompt: Twelve crayons are shared equally into 4 packs. How many crayons per pack?
steps: Make four receiving groups.
Three in each uses twelve because 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12.

items.prompt: Five packs each need 4 stickers. How many stickers are needed?
steps: Count five equal groups of four.

items.prompt: A class needs 18 cards and has 11. How many more cards are needed?
steps: The target eighteen contains the eleven already held.
18 − 11 = 7; eleven plus seven reaches the target.

items.prompt: Key ● = 1 packet. Paper: ● ● ● ●; Beads: ● ●. Which supply has more packets, and by how many?
steps: Read four paper packets and two bead packets.
4 − 2 = 2 extra paper packets.

items.prompt: A child plans 3 kits of 5 counters from 12 counters. Is the supply enough?
steps: Three kits of five require fifteen counters.
Fifteen minus twelve is three short.

worksheets.title: Connect and reason: A class supply plan
worksheets.directions: An adult may read all text aloud. Draw or use counters when helpful; all needed quantities are supplied. Explain your thinking in words, drawings, or number sentences. Work on a few tasks at a time. Point to a model or answer aloud if writing is a barrier; an adult may record the response.

items.prompt: A supply has 20 buttons. Pack them 4 per bag. How many full bags?
steps: Group the buttons in fours.
Five groups of four use twenty with none left.

items.prompt: Key ■ = 1 sheet. White: ■ ■ ■ ■ ■; Green: ■ ■ ■; Pink: ■ ■. How many white and pink sheets together?
steps: Select the five White and two Pink pictures.
5 + 2 = 7; the Green row is outside this question.

items.prompt: Two teams have 14 and 9 markers. How many markers must be added to the smaller supply to match?
steps: Find the difference between fourteen and nine.
9 + 5 = 14, so five additional markers make the supplies equal.

items.prompt: A class has 30 paper strips and uses 18 for a model. How many remain?
steps: Separate the used part eighteen from the whole thirty.

items.prompt: Four kits each need 2 brushes and 3 pencils. Find the total brushes and total pencils.
steps: Four groups of two brushes make eight.
Four groups of three pencils make twelve; keep the item types separate.

items.prompt: Key ★ = 1 vote. Paint: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★; Build: ★ ★ ★ ★. The class chooses the option with more votes. Which is selected?
steps: Paint has five votes and Build has four.
The supplied decision rule chooses the greater count.

worksheets.title: Use and check: A class supply plan
worksheets.directions: An adult may read all text aloud. Draw or use counters when helpful; all needed quantities are supplied. Explain your thinking in words, drawings, or number sentences. Work on a few tasks at a time. Point to a model or answer aloud if writing is a barrier; an adult may record the response.

items.prompt: A cupboard has 17 counters. Make 3 packs of 5 and leave the rest in the cupboard. How many remain?
steps: Three packs use 5 + 5 + 5 = 15 counters.
17 − 15 = 2 remain, as the plan permits.

items.prompt: A graph key is ● = 1 packet. A: ● ● ●; B: ● ● ● ●. Two packets are added to A. Give the new total and larger category.
items.answer: 9 packets total; A is larger with 5
steps: A changes from three to five; B stays four.
5 + 4 = 9, and five exceeds four.

items.prompt: A teacher has 18 stickers and wants 6 equal packs. A plan says 4 in each. Correct and check it.
steps: Six groups of four would need twenty-four, more than eighteen.
Six groups of three make eighteen exactly.

items.prompt: Design equal packs using all 16 counters, with more than one pack and more than one counter in each. Give one valid plan.
items.answer: For example, 4 packs of 4; 2 packs of 8 or 8 packs of 2 also work.
steps: Choose a group count and size that are both greater than one.
Their repeated-group total must be sixteen with no leftovers.

items.prompt: A child counts supply pictures and reports 10 items: Glue 2, Paper 5, Brush 4. Explain the check.
steps: Add the labelled counts: 2 + 5 + 4 = 11.
Compare that total with the report; ten leaves out one item.

items.prompt: A plan needs 4 packs of 3 cards. The graph key is ★ = 1 card and shows Red: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★; Blue: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ ★. Is the supply exact?
items.answer: Yes; both the supply and need are 12 cards
steps: The graph totals five red plus seven blue, twelve.
Four groups of three need twelve, so no cards are missing or left over.
